problems: The QBiC-SELEX results support in-vitro allele-preference hypotheses only; none establishes allele-specific TF occupancy in cells. The predicted alt preference therefore cannot yet be treated as a cellular effect.

MCF-7 ChIP evidence supports occupancy for ESR1, FOXA1, ZNF143 and JUN, but occupancy alone does not show that the variant changes binding. E25 and E26 also combine datasets with different peak/summit positions; those distances should not be treated as a direct comparison of TF candidacy.
TOX3 is the nearest protein-coding gene by TSS, but no direct variant-to-TOX3 regulatory link is shown. The variant does not overlap a SCREEN cCRE, and the nearest dELS is 38 bp away.

No cited evidence establishes an effect on breast-cancer risk or the direction of any transcriptional effect. The literature quotes with masked rs identifiers cannot be confidently mapped to this variant.

games.reason: Both TFs have MCF-7 occupancy near the variant and in-vitro models favor alt binding. ESR1 is better supported overall: it is more highly expressed in MCF-7, its mapped model shows a stronger alt-binding effect, and ReMap reports many ESR1 peaks containing the variant in MCF-7, compared with one ZNF143 peak. ZNF143’s summit is closer, but that alone does not outweigh the other evidence. Neither chain establishes a variant-to-TOX3 effect or breast-cancer risk.

Both chains have in-vitro predictions favoring alt binding and local MCF-7 occupancy, but ESR1 is more directly supported overall: it is more highly expressed in MCF-7 and has extensive ReMap support there, with 139 peaks containing the variant. ZNF143 has a closer reported summit, but its MCF-7 ReMap support is one peak. The ESR1 model also shows the larger predicted alt-binding effect. These data favor B, though neither establishes allele-specific binding in cells or a variant-to-TOX3 effect.

We found that CT (Cytocine-Thymine) and TT (Thymine -Thymine) genotypes, and T alleles of TOX3 rs[masked], were associated with BC risk (p = 0.034, p = 0.011, respectively).
SNP TOX3 rs[masked] was associated with positive progesterone receptors (PR) and triple-negative BC (TNBC) but not with estrogen receptor (ER) or HER2 reactivity.
TOX3 has been reported to be highly expressed in breast tumors and is closely related to estrogen receptors.
Our study demonstrated that TOX3 quantitatively and qualitatively stimulates estrogen synthesis by enhancing estrogen signaling pathway-related gene expression in ovarian granulosa cells.
Differences in panel performance influenced association signals, including breast cancer candidate loci such as FGFR2, TOX3, and ESR1.

We curated a panel of 15 breast cancer associated genes ( BRCA1, BRCA2, TP53, PTEN, CHEK2, ATM, CDH1, PALB2, LSP1, MAP3K1, NF1, RECQL, TOX3, FANCD2, RAD51C ) based on clinical and epidemiological relevance.

Moderate-risk genes ( PALB2, RAD51C, CHEK2 ) showed intermediate levels of pathogenicity, while low-risk genes such as RECQL, TOX3 , and FANCD2 were predominantly enriched for variants of uncertain significance.

Key examples include promoter mutations [e.g., rs[masked] (Mouse double minute 2 homolog gene; MDM2)], enhancer mutations [e.g., rs[masked] (thymocyte selection-associated high mobility group box family member 3 gene; TOX3)], and lncRNAs [e.g., HOX transcript antisense intergenic RNA (HOTAIR)] linked to progression, metastasis, and poor survival.
